intro: When you search for an estate planning advisor near me, you are likely thinking about how to organise your affairs for later life and inheritance, and you want someone local who can guide you through the options. Estate planning advisers help families plan for the future, often working alongside solicitors and financial advisers. We introduce you to a suitable UK professional who can discuss your needs and quote you directly.
need_heading: What people searching for an estate planning advisor near me usually need
need_lead: Most people looking for an estate planning advisor near me want clear, local guidance on organising their assets and plans for later life.
needs: You want to make or update a will but are unsure whether to use a solicitor, a chartered legal executive or an unregulated will writer.
You need to understand how your pension will pass on and whether it falls outside your will.
You are thinking about making gifts to family and want to keep proper records for inheritance tax purposes.
You are looking for advice on setting up trusts or other arrangements to protect assets for future generations.
You want a local adviser who can work with your existing solicitor or financial adviser to coordinate your estate plan.
context_heading: One key thing to understand about estate planning advice
context: Writing a will is not a reserved legal activity in England and Wales, so some will writers are not regulated. Solicitors (regulated by the SRA) and chartered legal executives (regulated by CILEx) are regulated, insured and covered by the Legal Ombudsman. Many specialists are also members of STEP or Solicitors for the Elderly.

When choosing a provider, ask whether they are regulated, whether they hold professional indemnity insurance and where your original will is stored. If you live in Scotland, make sure your adviser practises in the right jurisdiction, as succession rules differ.
tell_heading: What to tell iComply when enquiring
tell: Whether you already have a will and whether you are looking to make a new one or update an existing one.
The main assets you want to cover, such as your home, savings, investments or business interests.
Whether you have specific concerns about inheritance tax or passing on assets to children or grandchildren.
Any gifts you have already made and whether you have kept records of them.
Whether you are working with a solicitor or financial adviser already and want someone to coordinate with them.
Your location and whether you prefer to meet in person or are happy with telephone or video appointments.
questions: Are you regulated, and by which body?
Do you hold professional indemnity insurance?
Where will my original will be stored?
How do you charge for your services, and will you provide a written quote?
Do you have experience with estates that include pensions and gifts?
Will you work alongside my existing solicitor or financial adviser?

faqs.q: Do I need a solicitor to write a will?
faqs.a: Not necessarily. Writing a will is not a reserved legal activity in England and Wales, so you can use an unregulated will writer. However, solicitors and chartered legal executives are regulated and insured, which may give you more protection.

faqs.q: Can an estate planning adviser help with probate?
faqs.a: Some estate planning advisers can help with probate, but applying for a grant of probate on someone else's behalf for a fee is a reserved activity. Make sure the person you instruct is authorised to do this work.

faqs.q: How do I choose an estate planning adviser near me?
faqs.a: Ask about regulation, insurance and experience, and check whether they are members of a professional body such as STEP or Solicitors for the Elderly. It is also worth meeting them to see if you feel comfortable discussing your affairs.

faqs.q: What should I bring to my first meeting?
faqs.a: Bring details of your assets, any existing will, and information about gifts you have made. It also helps to have a rough idea of what you want to achieve, such as providing for family or reducing inheritance tax.

extra_heading: Choosing between local estate planning advisers
extra: Searching for an estate planning advisor near me usually means you want someone you could sit down with face to face, rather than a firm you found through a will-writing offer online. That is a sensible instinct, because estate planning often involves sensitive family conversations and documents you will want to revisit. It helps to think about what 'near me' really needs to mean for you: close enough to visit easily, or simply within reach for the occasional appointment.

Comparing advisers for this kind of work is less about finding the one with the loudest advert and more about matching their expertise to your circumstances. Ask what share of their work involves estates like yours, whether they work with pensions, trusts or gifts, and how they would coordinate with any solicitor or financial adviser you already use. A short first conversation will usually tell you whether they listen carefully and explain things in plain terms.

It is also worth being clear in your own mind about the difference between an estate planning adviser, a will writer and a solicitor. Some advisers focus on the wider plan and bring in regulated solicitors for the legal documents, while others draft wills themselves. Knowing which you are speaking to helps you ask the right questions about regulation, insurance and where your original will will be kept.

extra_faqs.q: Is an estate planning adviser the same as a solicitor?
extra_faqs.a: Not always. Some estate planning advisers work alongside solicitors and financial advisers rather than being solicitors themselves. Writing a will is not a reserved legal activity in England and Wales, so ask whether the person you speak to is regulated and by which body.

extra_faqs.q: Can I use an adviser near me if I live in Scotland?
extra_faqs.a: You can, but make sure they practise in the right jurisdiction. Scotland has its own rules on succession and confirmation, so an adviser used to the law in England and Wales may not be the right fit.

extra_faqs.q: What if I only want a simple will?
extra_faqs.a: That is still worth discussing with an adviser, because even a straightforward will can be affected by pensions, gifts and how assets are held. A brief conversation will help you judge whether you need wider estate planning or just a will.
